title: Why are the ribs bright?
prompt: On a fictional chest teaching image, ribs look lighter than the air-filled lungs. What produces that difference?
answer: Different X-ray attenuation along the beam path.
rationale: Bone attenuates more of the beam than air-filled lung. On the usual radiographic display this produces lighter bone and darker lung. These are projected shadows, not a direct photograph.

title: A larger-looking heart
prompt: A fictional portable AP chest image shows a larger cardiac silhouette than an earlier PA image. Does the apparent change alone prove true heart enlargement?
answer: No. Check projection and acquisition differences first.
rationale: AP geometry can magnify the cardiac silhouette. Comparing apparent size across AP and PA images without considering technique can mislead.

title: A normal bone image, persistent symptoms
prompt: In a fictional wrist lesson, a radiograph shows no visible fracture. Does this exclude a tendon injury?
answer: No. Radiographs have limited ability to show many soft-tissue injuries.
rationale: A radiograph answers some questions well but cannot establish that every tissue is normal. Further evaluation depends on the clinical examination and the question being asked.

title: One slice, two appearances
prompt: In the windowing lab, the same synthetic CT values look different when you change from a broad window to a narrow one. Has the tissue changed?
answer: No. The mapping from values to display shades changed.
rationale: A narrow window spreads a smaller input range across the available grayscale. Values outside that range are clipped at the display extremes. The original values remain unchanged.

title: Separating overlapping structures
prompt: Two structures overlap on a fictional frontal chest radiograph. What is the conceptual advantage of examining CT slices?
answer: Cross-sectional views separate anatomy by location through the body.
rationale: CT reconstructs measurements from many angles. Successive slices and reformatted planes help localize structures that overlap in a projection image.

title: Not all contrast is the same
prompt: A learner says that contrast for CT and contrast for MRI are interchangeable because both make anatomy easier to see. What is missing?
answer: The agent and imaging mechanism are different.
rationale: Iodinated agents commonly enhance CT by altering X-ray attenuation. Gadolinium-based agents commonly enhance MRI by changing magnetic properties. Screening is specific to the agent, patient and examination.

title: Bright on DWI
prompt: A fictional lesion is bright on a diffusion-weighted image. Can you call it restricted diffusion from that image alone?
answer: No. Review the ADC map and the other sequences.
rationale: DWI brightness can reflect T2 shine-through. Corresponding reduced ADC supports restricted diffusion, but the pattern still needs anatomical and clinical context; it is not a diagnosis by itself.

title: The implant card
prompt: A fictional patient brings an implant card marked MR Conditional. Does that mean scanning is allowed with any MRI setup?
answer: No. The exact device conditions must be checked and satisfied.
rationale: MR Conditional describes safety under specified conditions. Device identity, manufacturer labeling and the site's MRI safety process determine whether the proposed examination meets those conditions.

title: Blur across a sequence
prompt: A fictional MRI sequence has blurred tissue boundaries after movement. Should every indistinct edge be read as abnormal anatomy?
rationale: MRI collects data over time. Movement can reduce interpretability. Compare other sequences and assess technical quality before assigning significance to an apparent finding.

title: Red does not mean oxygenated
prompt: A fictional color Doppler display shows one vessel segment in red and another in blue. Does this identify arterial versus venous oxygenation?
answer: No. Read the color scale and flow direction relative to the probe.
rationale: Color Doppler encodes motion information. A color does not independently establish vessel identity or oxygen content; changing the display convention can reverse the colors.

title: Why use gel?
prompt: A fictional scanning demonstration compares dry probe contact with gel contact. Why does coupling gel help?
answer: It reduces intervening air between the probe and skin.
rationale: Air at the interface disrupts transmission into the body. Gel improves acoustic coupling so emitted sound and returning echoes can pass between the transducer and tissues.

title: An organ hidden by gas
prompt: During a fictional abdominal ultrasound lesson, bowel gas obscures part of an organ. Is the unseen region proven normal?
answer: No. An incomplete acoustic window limits the examination.
rationale: Gas can disrupt ultrasound transmission. Distinguish a structure that was assessed and appeared normal from a structure that was not adequately visualized.
